It worked fine. It also bugged me, because both of those hops are just processes on the same machine talking to each other over TCP. One of them is Nginx connecting to itself.
So I swapped both for Unix sockets. It's a small change, but the interesting part isn't speed. It's who gets to connect.

    H -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App["App"]
    C -->|"HTTP · loopback"| App
N -->|"SNI: custom domain · unix socket"| C["Caddy on-demand TLS"]
A loopback port is open to every process on the machine. If something else on the box gets compromised, it can talk to

just like Nginx does. That's not a big deal while those listeners are plain TLS endpoints, but I knew I'd want to add PROXY protocol next, and a listener that trusts a header from whoever connects is a bad idea. (That's the next post.)

A Unix socket is a file. To connect you need permission on it, and on the directory it lives in. So the filesystem becomes your access control, with no firewall rule or extra config. You also drop two arbitrary port numbers that someone, probably you in six months, will have to wonder about.
One directory for all of them
I put both sockets in the same directory, so there's one place to check and one permission rule to reason about:

echo 'd /run/app-sockets 0750 caddy www-data -' | sudo tee /etc/tmpfiles.d/app-sockets.conf
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create

You might wonder how Nginx creates a socket in a directory its workers can't write to. It doesn't need the workers for that. The master process runs as root and creates the listening sockets at startup. The workers, running as
, only have to walk into the directory and connect, and the group's read and execute bits cover that.
is tmpfs. The directory and any stale sockets disappear on reboot, and the tmpfiles rule recreates the directory at boot.

Sockets make sense when you control both ends and want the filesystem to decide who's allowed in. For the Nginx-to-Nginx and Nginx-to-Caddy hops, that's true. The app is a separate process with its own lifecycle, and it's also what
and health checks talk to. Keeping that boring is worth more to me than a slightly shorter path.
Don't expect it to be faster in any way you'd notice. You skip the TCP handshake and the kernel's bookkeeping on these hops. There are no ports involved, so there's no
pile on the closing side after a burst of connections. But it's bookkeeping, not bandwidth. I'd measure before claiming anything beyond that. If you want to see the

My stream block was opening TCP connections to Nginx itself and to Caddy, on loopback ports anyone on the box could reach. Here's the move to Unix sockets, the permissions that make it worthwhile, and what I left alone.
Multi-Tenant Custom Domains, without paying for Cloudflare for SaaS
, a SaaS that serves live countdown timer images for emails. Customers wanted
instead of our domain, which meant issuing and renewing TLS certs for domains I don't know in advance.

Cloudflare for SaaS solves this, but I wanted to keep it on the single server I already run. So I built it with Nginx and Caddy. This is the loop I went through: what I tried, what broke, and what the final setup looks like.

Gotcha: ACME challenges and scanner noise
HTTP-01 needs port 80 to reach Caddy for the customer domain, which the
block from Bug 1 handles. If issuance fails, check first that the customer's DNS actually points at your server.
tls-alpn challenge ... no information found to solve challenge for identifier:
in Caddy's logs every few days. Look at the

field: when it's empty, something connected with the ACME ALPN protocol but sent no hostname. Real validations carry the domain, so this is almost certainly a scanner, and Caddy is correctly refusing it.
A page that loads proves nothing. I checked each path separately, from a machine other than the server:

curl -sI https://timer.customer.com/        # customer-domain path
curl -sI https://app.example.com/           # main-app path
Both should answer over HTTPS with no certificate warnings. To inspect the certificate Caddy actually issued:
echo | openssl s_client -connect timer.customer.com:443 -servername timer.customer.com 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
That should show Let's Encrypt as the issuer, with dates that make sense.
Last, issue a certificate for a domain that has never touched the server and read Caddy's log:
